segments.text: Big idea. Daniel 4 is a pagan emperor's own decree. It records the king's boast, the sentence
pronounced from heaven, and his later acknowledgment that the Most High rules over earthly kingdoms
– Daniel 4, 30-37. From the Last Sitting – Sitting 3
In Chapter 3, God delivered his servants from the superheated furnace when Nebuchadnezzar
tried to compel worship. Now in Chapter 4, that same monarch learns firsthand that
the God of heaven alone establishes and overthrows thrones.
An Emperor's Open Confession – Daniel 4, 1-3, Babylon
Daniel 4 is unusual in the Bible. It keeps an official letter that a non-Jewish king
wrote in the first person. Nebuchadnezzar addresses,
"...all people, nations, and languages that dwell in all the earth," Daniel 4-1, compared
the decree of King Darius in Daniel 6, 25-27.
This is not a stone monument boasting of conquered lands or slaughtered enemies. It is a public
letter to all peoples, telling how the king was humbled and then restored. He had already
seen God's power in the dream of the great statue, Daniel 2, and in the rescue of the
three Hebrews from the furnace, Daniel 3. Now he writes to testify that no ruler holds
power by his own right. God gives it, and God can take it back.
"...to the intent that the living may know that the most high ruleth in the kingdom
of man, and giveth it to whosoever he will, and seteth up over it the basest of men."
Daniel 4, 17, KJV. Main Point 1. The Cosmic Tree in the Thesis of Thrones
Daniel 4, 10-27. The narrative begins with a disturbing dream. The king sees a colossal
tree standing at the center of the earth, reaching into the heavens, its foliage, sheltering
every creature and feeding all living flesh. Daniel 4, 10-12. Suddenly, a watcher, a holy
one, a commissioned heavenly messenger descends and commands. Hew down the tree and cut off
his branches, shake off his leaves, and scatter his fruit. Nevertheless, leave the stump of
his roots in the earth, even with a band of iron and brass, and let seven times pass
over him. Daniel 4, 14-16, KJV. Daniel interprets the dream with deep pastoral
sorrow. The immense tree is Nebuchadnezzar himself. Daniel 4, 20-22. A tree is a fitting
picture of a king. It is tall and strong, and it shelters everyone who lives under it,
as the king's rule sheltered his people. Because the king has grown proud, heaven
has decreed that he will be cut down, driven from human society and forced to live like
a wild animal until he learns the main lesson of this chapter, heaven rules. The chapter
states its main lesson three times, and the lesson is the same each time. The Most High
rules over all human power. The Most High ruleth in the kingdom of men, and giveth it to
whomsoever he will. Daniel 4, 17. Till thou know that the Most High ruleth in the kingdom
of men, Daniel 4, 25. Until thou know that the Most High ruleth in the kingdom of
men, Daniel 4, 32. Mercy Before Judgment. God did not carry out this sentence at once.
Daniel earnestly pleaded with the emperor, Break off thy sins by righteousness, and thine
iniquities by showing mercy to the poor, if it may be a lengthening of thy tranquility.
Daniel 4, 27. Nothing in the chapter says the king changed. At the end of twelve months,
he was walking in his palace in Babylon. Daniel 4, 29. And there he made the boast
of Daniel 4, verse 30. God's patience waded through those twelve months. Text,
The tree is the king. The watcher hues it down. The banded stump preserves mercy.
The thesis repeats three times. The Most High rules. We have come to the first checkpoint.
Main Point 2. The King's Boast and Humiliation. Daniel 4, 29-33.
A year after Daniel's plea, the king had still not turned from his pride.
He was walking in the palace of the kingdom of Babylon, Daniel 4, 29,
when his boast spilled out. Daniel 4, 30 names only Great Babylon, the city's famous works,
such as the blue tiled Ishtar Gate and the processional way that led to it,
have since been dug up. The boast was this. Is not this Great Babylon that I have built for
the house of the kingdom by the might of my power and for the honor of my majesty?
Daniel 4, 30, KJV. Back in Daniel 2, 37, Daniel had told him the God of heaven half given the
kingdom power and strength and glory. Pride is taking credit for what was received purely
as a divine gift. As the words left the king's mouth, a voice from heaven pronounced sentence.
Daniel 4, 31. Daniel records that the king was driven from human company and ate grass like an
ox while seven times passed over him. A time here is a year, so the sentence lasted seven
ordinary years. It had a set length and a purpose. The king was to learn that the most high
ruleeth in the kingdom of men. Daniel 4, 25. His hair grew like eagle's feathers
and his nails like bird's claws. Daniel 4, 32, 33. The account then says that his
understanding returned when he lifted his eyes to heaven. Daniel 4, 34. The chapter connects
the king's boast with the sentence he receives, then records his understanding returning after he
lifts his eyes to heaven. Daniel 4, 34, 35. The chapter gives its own reason for what happened
to the king, his pride in God's sentence. It does not give a medical explanation.
A reading rule. One king's lifetime, not 2520 years. Some people apply the year-day principle
to Daniel 4. This is the rule from sitting zero. In a symbolic vision, one prophetic day stands for
one year. They count a prophetic year as 360 days, 12 months of 30 days, and multiply by seven.
Seven times 360 is equal to 2520. That turns the seven times into 2520 years.
This does not fit the chapter for two reasons. The year-day rule belongs only to symbolic
visions, the kind full of beasts, horns, and other pictures, called apocalyptic visions.
Examples are Daniel 725's A Time and Times and the Dividing of Time, read with the 1260 days
of Revelation 12.6 and the 2300 days of Daniel 8.14. In those visions, the days are part of the
picture. The dream in Daniel 4 is a symbol. The tree stands for the king. But the chapter then
tells what happened to the king as history. All this came upon the king Nebuchadnezzar, Daniel 4.28.
It names the palace, the 12 months, and the throne he returned to. If the seven times were 2520 years,
Nebuchadnezzar would still be eating grass today. Instead, the king himself came back to
his throne in his own lifetime, Daniel 4.36. So, the seven times are seven ordinary years in one
man's life. We have come to the second checkpoint. Main point three. Understanding restored. Daniel
4.34-37. Restoration came only when the king looked beyond his own achievements.
And at the end of the days, I, Nebuchadnezzar, lifted up mine eyes unto heaven. And mine
understanding returned unto me, and I blessed the Most High, and I praised and honored him
that liveth forever, whose dominion is an everlasting dominion, and his kingdom is from
generation to generation. Daniel 4.34-37. The end of the days in the verse above is the end of the
seven times. The banded stump in the dream proved that God's judgment was tempered with mercy.
The mercy is concrete. The stump is left. And after the king lifts his eyes,
he receives his throne again. Daniel 4.36. Daniel explained the stump himself.
Thy kingdom shall be sure unto thee, after that thou shalt have known that the heavens do rule.
Daniel 4.26. The band of iron and brass is the dream's picture of that promise. A kingdom kept,
not ended. Upon his restoration, the emperor published his closing words of praise. To a
base means to bring low. Now I, Nebuchadnezzar, praise and extol and honor the king of heaven,
all whose works are truth and his ways judgment, and those that walk in pride, he is able to
a base. In plain words, pride took the king down, and lifting his eyes to God,
brought him back, because the Most High rules. Interpretation.
Daniel 4 answers one question. Who is the source of a kingdom, a career, or a life?
The chapter makes the answer one sentence and repeats it three times. Daniel 4.17.25.32.
The Most High Rules. The king learned it in this order. Heaven warned him before it judged him.
A full year passed between Daniel 4.27 and the boast of Daniel 4.30,
so the warning was real, and the patience was real. Then he said, I have built,
and the sentence fell. He lost his reason and lived like an ox. Notice where his reason came back,
not when the seven years ended, but when he lifted his eyes to heaven. Daniel 4.34.
The order is turn and then restore. The tree dream shows it step by step. The tree is the king,
Daniel 4.22. It is cut down because pride cannot be left in charge. The stump is left with a band
of iron and brass, and Daniel 4.26 explains that band. His kingdom would be sure to him again.
So the judgment was not the end of him. It was the limit set on him. A stump is a thing
still rooted. That is why the chapter ends with the king praising God instead of complaining.
He was not owed his throne. He was given it, and then given it again.
The bottom line is the same for an empire and for one person.
What you build is held on loan, and the loan is called in when you treat it as your own.
The king himself says that his understanding returned when he lifted his eyes to heaven
and praised the Most High. Daniel 4.34-37. Philippians 2.6-8 from the Apostle Paul's
Letter to the Church at Philippi shows Christ's humility as the opposite of the king's boast.
We have come to the third checkpoint. Main point four. The redemptive apex.
Christ, the true and humble king. Nebuchadnezzar's humiliation contrasts with the humility of Jesus
Christ. Daniel records the king's boast and judgment. Philippians 2.6-8 from the Apostle
Paul's Letter to the Church at Philippi describes Christ choosing the form of a servant.
Why does a lesson about a proud king turn to Christ? Because this chapter is about pride
and humility, and the New Testament answers both with him. The king was brought low
because he lifted himself up. Christ went low by his own choice.
1. The divine self-emptying. While Nebuchadnezzar walked in the palace and boasted,
Is not this great Babylon that I have built? Daniel 4.29-30. Jesus Christ, being in the form
of God, thought it not robbery to be equal with God, but made himself of no reputation
and took upon him the form of a servant and was made in the likeness of men. Philippians 2.6-7.
Christ did not hold on to his divine privileges. He willingly came down into human weakness to save
a human race that had turned against God. 2. Restoring the fractured image of God.
Daniel's account describes Nebuchadnezzar living like an animal during his humiliation.
Daniel 4.32-33. Pride brought a king down to that. Genesis 1.27 says people were made in
God's image, which means made to be like him in character, and pride damages that likeness.
In contrast, Philippians 2.6-8 describes Jesus humbling himself and taking the form of a servant.
Colossians 3.10 says the new man is renewed in knowledge after the image of him that created him.
And 2 Corinthians 3.18 says believers are changed into the same image from glory to glory.
Those verses of the repair this card is pointing at, God renews people into his own image.
3. True greatness found at the cross. Jesus taught his disciples,
Whosoever exalteth himself shall be abased, and he that humbleth himself shall be exalted.
Luke 14.11. The cure for the boast I have built is to look at the Son of God. He had every right
to claim glory, and he gave it up, even to death on the cross. Philippians 2.8. That is the
opposite of the king's boast. Take my yoke upon you and learn of me, for I am meek and lowly in
heart, and ye shall find rest unto your souls. Matthew 11.29. Christology. Christ the true and
humble king. Nebuchadnezzar walked in the palace and boasted, Is not this great Babylon that I
have built? Daniel 4.29-30. Christ, being in the form of God, made himself of no reputation
and took the form of a servant. Philippians 2.6-7. The emperor was humbled by force. The son
emptied himself willingly. Sin reduces humanity to beast-like pride. Christ restores the imago dei.
The new man is renewed in knowledge after the image of him that created him. Colossians 3.10.
And believers are changed into the same image, from glory to glory. 2 Corinthians 3.18.
Understanding returned when Nebuchadnezzar lifted his eyes.
The father highly exalted the son after obedient humility. Take his yoke upon you.
Learn of him who is meek and lowly in heart. The antidote to every I have built boast. Matthew 11.29.
